narrative:
The model predicted a 71% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is well above the acceptance threshold, your law school application was rejected.

The three factors that weighed most heavily in this decision were your LSAT score, your class ranking at the end of your third year, and your first-year class ranking. Your LSAT score of 25 was the strongest driver and pushed the prediction strongly toward failure; it sits far below the average of 37 among students who were accepted. Your third-year ranking in the third decile was the second most important factor and also increased the likelihood of failure, falling noticeably below the average ranking of roughly sixth decile for accepted students. Your first-year ranking in the fifth decile worked in the opposite direction, modestly lowering the risk of failure, yet it was not enough to offset the other two influences.

Taken together, these academic signals led the model to conclude that the risk of bar exam failure was too high for admission. 

To improve your chances, focus on raising your standardized test performance and strengthening your upper-year grades. Retaking the LSAT and enrolling in a structured bar-preparation course could meaningfully change future predictions. Consider reapplying once you have demonstrable improvement in these areas.
